paragraphs.text: Following things in order is the mother of good arrangement. It gives our subjects a clear appearance and face, and it keeps the minds of the listeners clear and free from confusion. So let us not abandon that order. Even if the readings take their own course, let us keep to the order of the story.

In the preceding discourses we set out, from the teaching of the Holy Spirit, how man was made, what honor he was given, what rank, and what dominion over the things of the world. Next came the deception in paradise, the judgment that followed the inquiry, and the sentence pronounced with loving-kindness.

After these things came the story of Cain and Abel. Outwardly both set about honoring God in the same way, but they undertook their service in very different dispositions. Both of them brought an offering. But the one man's offering had only the outward form of a gift, while the other's had the fitting disposition and honor as well. Then envy followed. For piety is always followed by envy from the wicked and by a crown from the judge of the contest. Abel was killed: the first herald of righteousness, the first to love piety and pursue it, the first to honor truth and to love and worship God in truth, the one who in many ways became an imitator of Christ.

For I find that holy Abel bore many images of Christ. Just as the Savior is the leader and the first righteous one of those renewed after the law, so Abel is the leader in righteousness of all the people of old. In the renewal of humanity which the Lord of all accomplished, you find nothing before the Lord's body; and in the ancient order of mankind you find no righteousness that shone out before Abel's. Abel is the leader of the righteous of old, and Christ is the leader of the new righteous and of the saints who are renewed in truth.

That is why the Savior fixed the memory of Abel as the beginning of all righteousness. For he says to the Jews: "Truly I tell you, all the righteous blood shed since the foundation of the world will be avenged on this generation, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar." He fixed as the beginning of righteousness Abel, the man plotted against by men but crowned by God.

And see the wonder of it. Because Abel was the first to contend on the side of righteousness, he was the first to be counted worthy of suffering for piety. He became an image of Christ, who suffered for the truth; and Abel's blood too was found to come near to the Lord's blood, having great closeness to it because of his faith.

The saving blood is, as it were, a school for the whole world: nothing teaches us piety like the Lord's blood, which uses the truth as its tongue. Abel's blood cried out, and Christ's blood cries out too. But the one cries out in accusation, while the other cries out bringing atonement to the world. Since the Lord's blood rang out like a trumpet to the ends of the earth, and Abel's blood appealed to God, the apostle, mentioning both bloods, by comparing them raised the truly higher blood to still greater heights. For he says: "We have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God the judge, the living one, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks better than Abel's." For the one speaks in accusation against murderers, while the blood of Christ speaks in intercession for sinners and brings atonement to the world. For the blood of Christ is the sprinkling of the whole world; the blood of Christ is the ransom of mankind. It "speaks better than Abel's," he says, inasmuch as the one accuses while the other pleads in our defense.

Abel's blood was also an image of the Lord's blood in this way. Adam sinned and fell under the curse of death: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall return." Abel received that sentence, though he had become righteous and had not fallen into sin; indeed he was attested by God's verdict and lived his life in holiness. Then the murderer Cain, by opening the gates of death, gave death an evil entry—or rather a good one. For see God's love for mankind. The condemned had not yet died, neither Adam nor Eve. Abel, who had not sinned, is the first of the condemned to die, God so arranging it that death should not gain a secure pasture; for the sure pasture of death is sin. So God arranged that, when piety was plotted against, the one who had not sinned should suffer on behalf of those who had been condemned, so that he might become an image of Christ, who bears death on behalf of sinners. For "he went to death for the sins of the people," Scripture says.

The name Abel, translated from the Hebrew language, means "mourning." For piety always groans in the present age; it mourns, it weeps, it laments sins, blasphemies, and injustices. So piety lives in mourning. But the Savior says: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted."

So when Abel had been killed—to keep to the order of the narrative—or rather when he had been crowned and taken the first rank in righteousness, another son, Seth, is born to Adam. His mother calls him Seth and explains the name, saying: "God has raised up for me another offspring in place of Abel, whom Cain killed." Seth is a recompense for the murder; for he was given in place of the son.

Seth means "watering." Pay attention here. Because, like water flowing over it, he refreshed the mother's thirsty root, worn out and deadened by grief, and made it put forth a shoot again, he was called Seth, that is, "watering."

And she says: "The Lord has raised up for me." She did not say "has raised" but "has raised up again." Resurrection is one thing, and raising up again is another. Resurrection is our first creation. For then God took dead earth and raised his creature up from the ground. He formed a living man, and our first forming was a resurrection. For he raised what lay cast down; he raised up the dust and changed it into human form. But the second resurrection, from the dead, is called a "raising up again," meaning a resurrection for the second time, since both then and now it is from the earth. The apostle says: "Being conformed to the death of our Lord, if somehow we may attain to his resurrection from the dead."

"God has raised up for me," she says, "another offspring in place of Abel, whom Cain killed." So Seth is born, as Scripture testifies, bearing a likeness matching Adam's. Cain was born firstborn, and he bore no resemblance to his father's face or image. Abel the righteous was born, and he had a form resembling Adam's, but even so not complete or truly like him. But Seth, whom God raised up in Abel's place, came forth, as Scripture says, "according to Adam's form and according to his image," having taken the very impress of his father's likeness.

Why did Scripture testify that he was made in Adam's image? Pay attention here, I beg you. Since this Seth was a type of the resurrection—for God raised him up again in Abel's place—he shows that the resurrection of the dead raises up our original forms and preserves the same images, and that nothing of a person's distinctive features perishes. "Adam," it says, "begot a son according to his image and according to his likeness, and named him Seth."

The heretics corrupt the teaching about the image. When we say of the Son, following the apostle, "who is the image of the invisible God," and, "who, being in the form of God," they say: "Does not this very word 'image' convince you that God is one thing and the image another? Is a man the same as his wax image?" But Scripture uses the word "image" in various senses. There is, for instance, an image that has form and shape, like a statue; but it has no pallor or fairness, no dark or light complexion. A wax image, on the other hand, represents appearance and colors. For it can portray the one-eyed man, the pale, the gray-haired, the dark, the ruddy, and the fair; the wax image imitates every color. A statue, however, cannot do this, but the wax image [?] has only shape and form. But the natural image, which bears the very character of the nature, is the one of which Scripture spoke: "Adam begot according to his form and according to his image."

Tell me, what is Adam's image? If Adam's image is his form, is the image of God a form? It is not his own substance of which the Son is the image [?]. "Adam," it says, "begot according to his form and according to his image." Therefore Christ is an image, not bearing form and shape, nor appearance and color; for the divine nature is incorporeal. You cannot speak of form in God, nor shape, nor appearance, nor color, for these belong to bodies. Then what is the true image of God? The one who is from him. The image of Adam is from Adam. The image is from the Father, begotten eternally from the Father who is without beginning.

And clearly showing the exactness of the image, he says: "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." According to the heretics, how can the like be seen through the unlike? You say the Son is less than the Father. So then, whoever has seen the one who is less than the Father has seen the greater!

Again, as you claim, the Savior can do nothing of himself. So then, whoever has seen the one who can do nothing has seen the one who can do all things. Whoever looks at the one under authority has seen the one who has authority of his own. Whoever looks at the creature has seen the Creator. Whoever looks at the one who once was not has seen the one who always is. This follows by ordinary reasoning. If he does not share equal honor, if he is not co-eternal, if he did not truly shine forth from the Father's nature, how is it that "whoever has seen me has seen my Father"?

"Adam begot according to his form and according to his image." Seth is born and preserves Adam's likeness. He begets a son named Enosh, of whom Scripture says: "He hoped to be called by the name of the Lord." Since we are lovers of God, we ought also to be lovers of the word—loving not the word from outside, but the divine Word, the teacher of souls, the light of every mind. What does this mean? Enosh was attested as one who "hoped to be called by the name of the Lord." Did Abel not call on the name of the Lord? If he did not, how did he offer gifts? Did Adam not call on the name of the Lord? Why was this not attested of anyone else?

So I will say something strange to my hearers, but true and free of danger, since it has Scripture as its witness. Enosh hoped to be called by the name of the Lord in this way: having become thoroughly righteous and having joined himself to God by piety, he hoped to be called by the name of the Lord God. "What prevents me," he says, "since I have loved God so, from being called god myself—not by usurpation, but by love?"

"He hoped to be called by the name of the Lord"—not simply "to be called," but "to be called by the name," so that he might be called both Enosh and god. Now Enosh means "man." Both Syriac and Hebrew interpret it so: Enosh means "man." So he hoped to be both man by nature and god by grace.

So this Enosh was called god. All the people of that time saw him and said: "Truly he is worthy of God; truly this is the form of God." Those born from him thereafter were called sons of God. Those of the line of Enosh who kept piety were thereafter called sons of God—of the God who is not offended but rejoices in this special relationship and welcomes the kinship of the pious. "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High."

From the time Cain received the curse, the two tribes were divided, that of Seth and that of Cain. The sons and descendants of Cain were called sons of men, and the sons and descendants of Seth were called sons of God. God wanted this righteous race of Seth, whom he raised up in Abel's place, not to intermarry with the offspring of Cain, just as he commanded the Jews not to give their daughters to foreigners or to take wives from the daughters of foreigners. So he wanted them kept apart; for God was gradually consuming the generation of Cain.

Pay attention now, I beg you. Cain evidently had scarcely seven successors, that is, seven generations, and after that he was consumed, as his line died out. Only daughters were born to the race of Cain, while males multiplied among the sons of God. Wishing to cut the sinews of the memory of the wicked and lawless man, God gradually cut off the male stock, and a few women were left among them, whom God knew to be capable of being ruled and not of ruling.

He did the same in the case of the Midianites. For when God commanded through Moses that all the Midianites be taken [?], he says: "But keep alive their virgin daughters," since the woman did no harm in the way of impiety; for she would be ruled and not rule. So just as he then commanded the women to be spared and the men to be killed, so he pronounced sentence against the male succession of the line of Cain. Since Cain had played the man against the righteous person of Abel, God cut off that manly spirit and reduced the line to weak and lowly women.

"When the sons of God saw," it says, "that the daughters of men were beautiful"—meaning: those who had been forbidden to have them mingled with them. "For they chose," it says, "and took wives for themselves"—not following the law. God does not blame them for taking wives, but for taking them for themselves. "They took," it says, "from all whom they chose." Since there were no men left, they took the women like captives and divided them up, not by the law of marriage but with the indifference of licentiousness.

Pay attention, then. So Scripture says: "And it came to pass, when the sons of men became many and daughters were born to them"—meaning: the male succession was cut off among them, and only the female remained. Then it adds: "When the sons of God saw the daughters of men, they took for themselves from all whom they chose."

We have not drawn these distinctions without reason. For some have thought that the sons of God are the angels, and say that angels came down and had intercourse with women, from whom the giants were born. This is entirely false. It is a myth—or rather, weakness of mind. For how could a bodiless angel have intercourse with a body, when they have neither the same members nor the same desire?

But let us grant, following the myth, that they were angels. Angels are spirits and fire, mighty and invincible in power. The women suffered violence from angels. When the flood came, why did it kill men and not angels? Did some sin and others get condemned? Surely those who suffered violence ought to have been pitied and the wrongdoers punished. Then, when the flood came, what harm did the water do to the angels? Spirits are not drowned in water. Yet the humans who suffered violence were drowned, and the angels who did the violence were saved. This sequence of events does not fit the supposed order of violence; those who suspected such a thing suspected wrongly.

Let us see what the judge says. "God saw the earth," it says, "and it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way on the earth." What does that have to do with angels? "My spirit shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh." If angels sinned, why does he blame men? But the name "giants" misleads some. "If those who were with the women were not angels," they say, "where did the giants come from?" By "giants" Scripture does not mean some strange formation or strange shape; it calls heroes, warriors, and mighty men giants. Scripture testifies to this: "Behold," it says, "the Lord will take away from Judea and from Jerusalem the strong man and the strong woman, the strength of bread and the strength of water, the giant and the strong man." What would a giant be doing in Jerusalem?

That the giants were men born of men, and not a Greek fiction or a mythical drama, Scripture again testifies. "Noah," it says, "had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham begot Canaan. Canaan begot Nimrod. He was a giant hunter before the Lord." See: the father was a man, the grandfather was a man, and the one born was a giant. Then too in the Old Testament the spies say to Moses: "We went into the land, and we were like locusts before them, and we saw giants." And they say who the giants were: "We saw the race of Anak." We say the same in ordinary speech: "a hero of a man," "an extraordinary man," "a giant of a man," not meaning that he has a nature different from ours, but expressing something manly and heroic in his soul. So the story of the giants is not a tale of war against the gods; rather, Scripture called tall heroes giants. For God made the sons of Seth like this, tall, and the sons of Cain short and mean, so that the difference might be visible even in their appearance: how the blessed are raised up on high while the cursed are brought low.

So, to show again that giants are not a drama of impiety or mythology, the prophet David says of the sun: "His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit to the end of heaven. He will rejoice like a giant to run his course."

So the giants were not born of angels, but of men; they were tall men, handsome in body and renowned for their beauty. Abandoning the order of their ranks, they divided up the women in disorder. God accuses them and says: "My spirit shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh."

The Manichaeans seize on this saying. "You see," they say, "where there is flesh, which comes from matter, God does not rest." Then God rests in no one, for we all have flesh. Again, if "My spirit shall not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh" is the saying of one who hates the flesh, how is it that Scripture says elsewhere: "I will pour out my spirit on all flesh"? By "flesh" Scripture does not mean the visible body; it calls "flesh" the person who is immoderately attached to the body and neglects the soul. Just as we say of a wise man, "He is all mind," not because he has no body but because he is wholly occupied with wisdom, so Scripture calls "flesh" the one who always attends to the body and gives no thought to the soul—not because he ought not to have flesh, but because he ought not always to be pampering the flesh and neglecting the soul.

For what we are asking is a matter of judgment: how much one should care for the soul, and how much for the body. Surely God does not want us not to care for the body; rather, he wants us not to neglect the soul and fail to care for it under the pretext of caring for our bodies. Consider ordinary usage too. I know that many, especially those eager to find fault, seize on illustrations as being lowly. But my aim is to set up the picture. Even if I use everyday illustrations, it is the truth that we are seeking.

Often at banquets we mix wine for ourselves. If it does not get as much water as it needs, we immediately say: "It's all neat wine"—not because it has no water, but because it does not have as much as it should. Someone else has put in a lot of water and little wine, and we immediately say: "It's all water"—not because it has no wine, but because it does not have the right proportion. So when Scripture says of someone, "He is all spirit," it is not because he has no flesh, but because the grace of the Spirit [?] abounds in him. Again, when Scripture says of someone, "He is all flesh," it is not because he has no spirit, but because he has given the greater share to the flesh.

Why, brothers, do the Scriptures call fornicators "lovers of women"? "And Solomon," it says, "was a lover of women." Yet the chaste man loves his own wife. Why then is the man devoted to his own wife not called a lover of women, though he loves his own wife? Because where there is law, where there is measure, where there is the marriage bond, excess is cast out, and he is called chaste even though he has a wife. So it is excess that is hated, while measure is honored.

Does God want the body to get the better of the soul? If someone says of a person, "He is all spirit," that is praise of the man; but if you hear, "He is all flesh," that is blame of the one so described. Paul says to the disciples, since they were devoted to the Spirit: "You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit." Were they then without flesh? No; but because, though they wore flesh, they cared less for it and more for the Spirit, he calls them not in the flesh. And today, if I see someone who was given a task and neglected it, I say at once: "You are not here with me"—not because he is not there, but because he is not present in his eagerness. Truly God saw wickedness gaining the upper hand.

We must know that neither vice nor wickedness, nor anything that is thought or said to be evil, has a stable existence or a nature of its own; it is a perversion of the good, just as vinegar has no nature peculiar to itself. For there is not a vine for wine and another plant for vinegar; vinegar is a perversion of wine. In the same way adultery is a perversion of marriage. For we know, brothers, that vinegar does not lose the appearance of wine; it keeps the look of wine and loses only its quality. Whether it comes from golden wine or from dark wine, it keeps the color. So too adultery and fornication do not obliterate the appearance of the chaste; they wear the face of chastity but do the deeds of lawlessness. It is like the perversion of wine.

And so that you may learn that we did not use this image idly, but that evil really is a perversion of the true vine, God says to the people through the prophet Jeremiah: "Thus says the Lord: I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true. How have you turned to bitterness, you alien vine?" Surely God does not blame the tree for its nature.

Did he give marriage and then accuse marriage? He formed man and said: "Let us make him a helper like him." And would he call the helper he made a plotter? If you keep the law, you have a helper; if you pervert the law, the helper becomes a plotter against you.

And pay attention. Paul says, "Marriage is honourable, and the bed undefiled in all things; but God will judge fornicators and adulterers." Learn from this the difference in the matter. Do marriage, fornication and adultery each look different? Is it not the same act? Are they not the same members? Is fornication done with some members, adultery with others, and marriage with others still? Are they not the same members? Is it not the same act? But the law is not the same. The one who does the act is punished and judged.

The judge, the law, stands by. If it is a marriage, it comes along and honours the marriage; if it is an unlawful union, the judge at once sharpens the sword and cuts off its boldness. In the one case it joins in carrying the wedding torches, since it commanded the marriage itself; but adultery, which does not please it, it punishes. It honours what is lawful, but wherever it finds the law perverted, it is provoked. Do you see that evil is not a nature, but that evil is a perversion of the good?

In the same way Christ, to show how he honours marriage, which he made, and punishes adultery, which he did not make, pronounces against adulterers, saying, "Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." But where he found a lawful marriage, he not only honoured the thing but was even found among the invited guests. "There was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and Jesus was there." The Lawgiver saw the law and honoured it; he saw the thing and did not flee from it. And let no one say, "Did God, so great as he is, really have to go to a wedding?" It was no disgrace for a wedding to take place with God present. When God brought Eve to Adam, he was not ashamed to give away the bride; will the Lawgiver then be embarrassed to be present? I say these things to [?]

[?] those who fled for refuge. Then the flood overtook them, and nothing found outside the ark was saved. The coming of Christ will overtake us, and no one found outside the Church is saved. The Lord of all bears witness to this, saying, "As it was in the days of Noah: they were eating, drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the flood came and took them all away—so will the coming of the Son of Man be." You see the image shining clearly, and the truth unforced.

But a separate discourse will be set aside for the flood, so that we may go through the whole sequence in due order and leave nothing in the divine Scriptures unexamined. This, however, I will say and propose: every good work has a face and can show itself openly.

No one is ever ashamed of righteousness; it may be attacked, but it cannot be put to shame. Godliness cannot be put to shame. Paul was persecuted, but he was not ashamed; he was bound, but he was not abashed. And he says, boasting, "It is for the hope of Israel that I wear this chain," but I am not ashamed of it. For the chains were not the penalty for wrongdoing but the praise of godliness. That is why Paul takes pride in it, saying, "Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ." Anyone else, if he is put in chains, wants no one to find out; Paul was put in chains, and he is distressed if everyone does not find out.

Look, then. God found fault with disorder, lawlessness and excess. Here the fables of the stage-players are refuted—and by stage-players I mean all who tell lies. When the flood came, where were the nativities of the stars? When the flood came, where did the fate determined by the course of the stars go off to? If the stars were the same then as now, they would have brought about the same results, since they kept the same course.

Yet a little infant was destroyed before its time. The star meant him to live many years. How then was he conceived? And if the nativity passed a single sentence against all the infants, why did these things not happen at every time? For if the course is always the same, why do they speak alike of things that do not come out alike? Does everything happen by nativity?

Before the knowledge of Christ, many generations and ages ran their course. Where were the stars that make Christians before Christ's coming? Where now are the stars that make paganism? Were there no pagans after Christ, and no Christians before Christ? Where is the nativity of the stars? We know, brothers, many strange things that run contrary to what is usual. Since they say that being born rich or poor, king or ruler, chaste or adulterer comes from one's nativity, I ask: is the chaste man a fixed thing, and have these things been revolving in human life from eternity? But Christianity is something that once did not exist and has now begun. And paganism once existed and has now been extinguished. Christianity once appeared, and it has shone forth. Where is the course of the stars that extinguished the one and made the other shine out? Now, by the grace of Christ, there are places of ascetic life in many lands, where people take pride in living by the Gospel. The stars that produce chastity—where were they then? I say these things to show that it is not the course of one's nativity, nor chance, nor fate, but that a good way of life bears good fruit and wicked conduct comes to an evil end.

God is long-suffering—not in the sense that he nurses his anger long, but in the sense that he is far removed from anger. I said it long ago: if you see God threatening, he wants to save; if you see God keeping silent about sins, understand that he intends to punish. When he threatens, he wants to save; when he keeps silent, he means to punish. I have said it, and yet I say it again: he proclaimed destruction to Nineveh and showed mercy; he kept silent about the Sodomites and destroyed them.

If you see yourself disciplined for a sin, understand that God is taking hold of you. Do not say, "It is because God hates me that I suffer such things." If you see yourself sinning and suffering nothing, say, "God has turned away from me. I do not like it that he is so patient. I have sinned much, and he has disciplined me neither with sickness nor with fever. Very likely he is saving me for a greater evil." For it is God's way to correct and discipline those he loves, so that they may escape the punishment to come.

It is God's way to punish the godly at once if they sin, so that they do not go on to a greater evil. He lays his hand on the righteous man who commits small sins, so that he may not fall into great ones. He lets the ungodly man go on stumbling many times, since his sins do not deserve the present punishment but a greater one.

David says of Moses and Aaron: "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call on his name: they called on the Lord, and he answered them; he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud. O God, you were gracious to them, and you took vengeance on all their deeds." By this he showed that he loved them in punishing their failings. Elsewhere, wishing to show the height of his indignation as he rebuked the people's sin, God says, "Therefore thus says the Lord: I will not visit your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery"—meaning: I no longer care about you, I do not look into your sins, I do not visit the adulterer in order to correct him. Do you see that overlooking is a sign of wrath, while disciplining is a sign of love for humankind?

God, then, wants to discipline us with threats so that we may escape punishments. God can make the threat serve for our correction, so that we are chastened by word and not by experience, so that there may be tears of repentance and not tears of torment. The one who pleads weeps, and the one who is beaten weeps; but the tears of those who plead are one thing, and the tears of those being flogged are another. The tears of repentance are the spices of godliness. For if the trees in the forest drip—some storax, others various spices—and the tears of trees produce perfumes, will not the tears of repentance become the spices of godliness?

May God, then, grant us to repent in truth, to be released from our sins, and to receive eternal joy in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom be glory, honour and worship to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.
